Stevensville.wildlife_intro:
Stevensville is Kent Island's historic center — the community at the foot of the Bay Bridge, where a preserved old-town grid of homes sits among marinas, boatyards, and the subdivisions that have spread down both shores of the island. Kent Island is nearly surrounded by water, and its wildlife moves along the shorelines: raccoons commute the bulkheads and marsh edges, denning in the crawlspaces and attics of the older homes near the old town and the waterfront communities alike.

Bats summer in the older rooflines and in the quiet attics of seasonal homes, squirrels work the canopy streets of the established neighborhoods, and skunks and opossums den under the raised cottages and porches near the water. The island's marshes hold muskrat and abundant bird life, and the occasional snake in a waterfront yard is usually a harmless waterside species — protected regardless, and identified before anything is done. Stevensville's bridge-side location means many homes are second homes or rentals, and the seasonal-occupancy problem is the island's signature: sealing before the quiet season, every year, is what separates the maintained waterfront house from the recurring emergency.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Queenstown chimney?
faqs.a: Yes — spring raccoon mothers choose uncapped chimneys across Queen Anne's County. Our crew checks whether pups are present before anything moves, removes the family together whenever we can, and fits a proper chimney cap so the same chimney is not a den again next spring.

faqs.q: When is wildlife pressure worst in Queenstown?
faqs.a: Spring denning and the fall push indoors are the two busy waves in Queen Anne's County, with bat colonies and mole damage peaking in summer. If you are hearing noise or seeing digging in Queenstown, calling at the first sign almost always makes for a simpler, cheaper job.

faqs.q: Rats are around my Grasonville home near the marinas — what does control involve?
faqs.a: Around the Kent Narrows marinas and seafood blocks, Norway rats live on fish waste and shelter in the nearest structures — crawlspaces, boathouses, and the wall voids of older buildings. Control is a program: burrow and run mapping, trapping on the active sign, sealing the foundation penetrations the rats use, and addressing the food source with the neighboring property where that is the driver. Maryland does not require a Wildlife Damage Control Permit for rat work, so judge any provider on the thoroughness of that program rather than a license claim. Single-visit rat promises on a working waterfront are not honest; we will give you the realistic schedule up front.

An inland neighborhood home with squirrels at the gable vents is a standard exclusion. Waterfront crawlspace work costs more than the same work inland because the screening has to be specified for brackish conditions to last. We inspect the water side first, explain what we find in order of importance, and give the complete figure before removal or sealing begins.

Grasonville.wildlife_intro:
Grasonville sits on the mainland side of the Kent Narrows, Queen Anne's County's working waterfront of marinas, seafood businesses, and charter boats, with residential neighborhoods spreading east toward Prospect Bay and the Route 50 corridor. The Narrows concentrates everything: marsh, marinas, restaurants, and homes within a few hundred yards of each other, and the raccoons and rats work the whole circuit nightly.

Raccoons den in the attics and crawlspaces of the waterfront homes and raid the marina blocks; rats hold the restaurant and dock areas where fish waste is steady; bats summer in the older rooflines; and the inland neighborhoods toward the highway get the suburban set — squirrels in the maturing trees, groundhogs on the open lots, skunks under the decks. Osprey platforms and marsh birds are the visible waterfront, but the calls come from below the roofline and under the house. Grasonville inspections start at the water side and work inland, because on the Narrows the animal pressure arrives from the marsh and the docks, and the openings facing them are the ones that fail first.

faqs.q: Why do Chester homes get raccoons in the crawlspace so often?
faqs.a: Chester's neighborhoods sit between the Chester River shore, Crab Alley Bay, and interior marsh, so raccoons reach most houses within a short shoreline walk. The crawlspaces of the area's raised and ranch-style homes offer exactly what a raccoon wants in March: dry, dark, and quiet, with vent covers that salt air has been weakening since installation. We remove the animals using the space — a spring check for pups comes first — and rebuild every vent and door with framed, anchored, corrosion-resistant screening. One unaddressed vent on the marsh side is all a Chester raccoon needs, so the inspection covers the full perimeter, not the side with the tracks.

faqs.q: Do groundhogs cause problems on Kent Island, or is it all raccoons?
faqs.a: Groundhogs are a real Kent Island problem away from the immediate shoreline, where Chester's interior lots and field edges give them the dry, diggable ground they need. Burrows under sheds, decks, and the occasional slab undermine structures and expand each season a system goes untreated. We trap at the active entrances through the warm season and backfill and screen once the system is empty. The shoreline lots see fewer groundhogs and more raccoons and skunks; the interior lots reverse the ratio — which is why the inspection starts by reading your lot's position on the island.

Chester.wildlife_intro:
Chester is Kent Island's eastern community, across the Kent Narrows from Grasonville, where subdivisions and waterfront neighborhoods line the Chester River and Prospect Bay shores and the island's interior carries a mix of established housing and open ground. It is quieter and more residential than the bridge end of the island, and its wildlife pattern is the waterfront-suburb standard at full strength.

Raccoons are the headline animal, living in the marsh and shoreline woods and denning in the chimneys, attics, and crawlspaces of the neighborhoods along Crab Alley Bay and the river shore. Squirrels work the maturing canopy in the older sections, bats take the larger attic peaks near the water in summer, and skunks and groundhogs divide the yards between them — skunks under the decks, groundhogs along the open field edges at the island's interior. Chester homes sit close to serious habitat on nearly every street, so the sealing standard here is the waterfront standard: corrosion-resistant materials, every low opening accounted for, and no assumption that a quiet season means a sealed house.
